Photograph: Laura Bargfeld/AP View image in fullscreen The South Chicago Chapel, where the bodies were found. Photograph: Laura Bargfeld/AP Chicago Remains of 56 people found decomposing at Chicago funeral home Officials describe ‘deplorable conditions’ at home run by pair linked to crematory closed due to mishandled remains Associated Press Fri 7 Aug 2026 20.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The remains of 56 people were found improperly stored and decomposing on Thursday at a Chicago funeral home run by a couple who previously operated a crematory that was similarly shut down because of mishandled remains, authorities said. Illinois state officials, meanwhile, suspended the license of one of the funeral home’s directors, alleging bodies were being kept in an unrefrigerated area in “deplorable conditions”. The discovery came months after neighborhood residents began noticing a “stench” emanating from the funeral home, which led some to complain to the city. The Cook county medical examiner’s office said it was notified by state and local officials that bodies were being stored improperly at South Chicago Chapel, and investigators and forensic pathologists were dispatched Thursday. The remains were in various states of decomposition, officials said. “Staff is assessing the conditions of the remains, searching for documentation regarding identification of the decedents as well as death certificates. This process could take several days to ensure proper disposition,” the medical examiner’s office said in a statement, adding that family notifications will be made following the identifications. Police said on Friday that their preliminary statement on the case incorrectly said that fire department officials declared the scene a hazardous materials incident. No arrests have been announced, but city police said detectives are investigating. Messages for the funeral home were left by phone and through its website on Friday. Later Friday, a small number of residents and people seeking information about their deceased loved ones gathered in front of the brick-walled funeral home, which is on a South Chicago street lined with trees, homes and businesses. Latasha Johnson, 55, said her mother’s funeral was held at South Chicago Chapel on Thursday before authorities arrived and she later heard of their gruesome discovery. She said authorities told her that her mother’s body would have to undergo an autopsy and she would have to identify the remains in a day or two. “I’m discombobulated,” she said. “My heart is broken.” Blaise Von Bruchhaeuser, who described herself as a community advocate for the neighborhood, said it was upsetting that complaints about a terrible odor had been made for months before the decomposing bodies were found. State business records show that funeral director Johanna Morgan incorporated South Chicago Chapel in 2022 and her funeral director’s license was temporarily suspended on Wednesday. The state department of financial and professional regulation said the license suspension was due to “a finding that respondent’s continued practice is a danger to the public safety, interest and welfare due to respondent allowing multiple decedents to be kept in an unrefrigerated area with deplorable conditions including rodent infestation, causing decomposition and maggot infestation of the bodies”. The state business records also list Clark Morgan, who state officials say is Johanna Morgan’s husband, as the funeral home’s president. The department of financial and professional regulation said Clark Morgan’s funeral director license was revoked in 2024 for practicing with an expired license and “unprofessional conduct” that it did not specify. Funeral home owners also ran crematory that was shut down by the state State comptroller Susana Mendoza said Friday that Johanna and Clark Morgan previously ran a crematory in Chicago Heights, south of Chicago, which had its license revoked last year after authorities discovered improperly stored bodies and hundreds of cremated remains that had never been returned to their families. “Horrified. Again,” Mendoza said in a statement. “The discovery of decomposing remains waiting to be laid to rest this week at a South Side funeral home is heartbreaking and an abomination. These are people – someone’s mother, father, sister, brother, child or friend, and they deserve better.” Both Johanna and Clark Morgan are listed in Cook county court records as defendants in connection with lawsuits involving Heights Crematory in Chicago Heights, south of Chicago. Messages were left on Friday at phone listings for the Clarks and an attorney listed in records as their business agent. Public records indicate the Clarks live in the Chicago suburb of Evergreen Park. The case is the latest in a series of incidents involving mishandled remains over the past three years. Last month, police arrested two men in Pueblo, Colorado, for allegedly mishandling at least two dozen decomposing bodies and other remains found behind a hidden door in a funeral home. That followed the discovery of 18 bodies in various stages of decomposition at a funeral home in Georgia in 2024. In 2023, nearly 200 decomposing bodies were found in a building in Colorado, and another 31 decomposing bodies were discovered at an Indiana funeral home. Photograph: Jon Pountney View image in fullscreen Jon Pountney was one of two photographers to witness the final days inside Tata’s last blast furnace. Photograph: Jon Pountney Wales Eerie silence and ‘still surviving’: what happened next after steel town’s last blast furnace shut down Exhibition in Port Talbot is part of project exploring how communities experience endings and transitions Bethan McKernan Wales correspondent Wed 12 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google M argaret Heggett, 95, does not remember a time when Port Talbot was ever quiet. Born and raised in the shadow of the steelworks, with a father, brother and husband who worked there, she never imagined what the town could look or sound like without its blast furnaces. “I’m not saying it was beautiful, but there were jobs. We did know the closure was coming and we have to move with the times but it’s affected the town a lot and it’s very sad,” she said. The south Wales town, one of the most deprived in the UK, is still grappling with the closure of the blast furnaces at its Tata Steel plant, which shut down in 2024 after more than 100 years, costing nearly 3,000 jobs. The transition has been difficult, with knock-on effects for supply chain workers and local businesses. Now, two years after the last blast furnace fell silent, an exhibition is telling the story of the closure and what has happened to the town since. View image in fullscreen The steelworks seen from the mountains overlooking Port Talbot. Photograph: Jon Pountney Steeling Ourselves , created by the Rhondda-based photographer Jon Pountney, combines photography and portraits of Port Talbot with interviews with the people living there, celebrating their “strength, creativity and determination to shape the future while preserving the memories and experiences that matter”. On display at the Plaza, a community hub, the exhibit is part of After the End, a research project by Exeter, Oxford and Liverpool John Moores universities exploring how communities experience endings and transitions. The research is intended to contribute to wider arguments about the social impact of major industrial changes, and to keep local voices in the conversation about regeneration strategies. For many interviewees, the silence after the last blast furnace shut down was eerie. “I used to camp out at night and the light was better than the northern lights,” one contributor said. “When you’re making iron, there’s 1,000-degree heat that lights the sky up and the shadow changes and it’s like a show, you know, and that’s what we were brought up on. I loved that.” View image in fullscreen A woman sunbathing on a beach with the works in the distance. Photograph: Jon Pountney Pountney was one of two photographers to witness the final days inside Tata’s last blast furnace before it closed. The exhibit also captures the beats of life in Port Talbot – friends messing about near the water, camping chairs on nearby Aberavon beach, terrace streets, pushchairs, meadows and wildlife – with the huge steelworks site almost always present in the background. Heggett said: “When I was asked to take part in the project, I’d had a glass of wine, so I thought ‘why not?’. It’s been lovely to reflect on.” View image in fullscreen Margaret Heggett, 95, was photographed for the project. Photograph: Jon Pountney People in the town felt strongly that the blast furnace closure did not mean “writing off their community”, said Patricia Kingori, a professor of global health ethics at the University of Oxford and lead researcher on After the End. “The exhibition is really rooted in hearing the experiences of people who had this ‘ending’ imposed on them, and what we can learn from them … The pace of change is such that we haven’t really reconciled yet what work and labour will look like in the future,” she said. “Port Talbot is the canary in the coalmine. The conversations the town is having are going to be repeated in all places and walks of life at some point.” Tata Steel is transitioning to a greener electric arc furnace, although the project has been hit by delays and the plant is expected to employ a fraction of the workforce it once did. “You can live the dream from Port Talbot,” one interviewee in the project said. “We’ve insisted upon that and the fact that we’re still surviving … being creative and doing all these positive things, shows that it’s actually true.” Explore more on these topics Wales Steel industry Photography Exhibitions news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

Emma Grunwald / The Westerly Sun Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save STONINGTON — Local retired couple Amy Fraher and Kathy Jones have opened a boutique fitness studio together, after overcoming cancer, to provide a supportive space for older adults to build strength, improve balance, and find community. “So many people say, ‘I should have done this before. I didn’t know how to do it. I didn’t know where to go.’ So we’re creating a place where people can learn how to do this at any age,” co-owner Amy Fraher said. Fraher, 64, and her wife, Kathy Jones, 77, officially opened “We Lift Heavy” in February of this year. Fraher leads the strength training sessions, while Jones, a certified yoga instructor, runs the yoga sessions. Fraher and Jones hosted a class of about five women in their 60s and into their 80s for a typical Tuesday morning strength training session, guiding clients through an interval-style workout with exercises including wall ball slams, gorilla rows, planks, Romanian deadlifts, leg presses, and hip adductions. Participant Laura Lynch-Young, 74, said she had previously worked out at the local YMCA but wanted a spot that offered more individualized attention. “I wanted to seek out a trainer who could pretty much guide me and keep me from making the wrong moves,” she said. “I just have better energy. I really look forward to coming to the gym. It's the first time in my life I've ever known how to use machines correctly. And that really takes a lot of intimidation out of going to a gym,” she added. Fraher explained that her inspiration for the studio came after her passion for fitness was reignited during her recovery from stage 4 ovarian cancer about three years ago. “I went through chemo, the whole thing. And now I feel great,” Fraher said in a joint interview with Jones after the class. When her cancer went into remission, Fraher was motivated to start exercising again. “All I wanted to do was work out because I knew my body wasn’t the same,” she said. “I was just in this place of, like, I don't really know who I am anymore, kind of, because I had been sick.” After becoming an avid member of the local YMCA in Mystic, a staff member encouraged Fraher to become a trainer. She gained experience there before deciding to open her own space with Jones, realizing some YMCA customers were looking for something different “Something more personal, clean, boutique,” Fraher said. Using seed money from her mother’s passing, Fraher and Jones rented the empty commercial space on River Rd. and bought the equipment. “To be honest with you, our model isn't to get huge,” Jones said. “Both of us like teaching, and we actually both have had teaching careers before we went into this.” Before retiring, Jones had been a professor in the Women’s Studies department at San Diego State University, while Fraher taught Business and Crisis Management. Fraher had also served as a helicopter pilot in the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps earlier in her career.​ In addition to creating a space to work out and get fit, they want the space to become a supportive environment for members to discuss their health or other issues. “One of our members just recently got diagnosed with cancer and she came, and she was talking about it,” Fraher said. “It felt good that she felt this was a place where she could talk to people about it, and she knew that we knew what it felt like. We can say, ‘Look, this sucks, but you're gonna get through it, you know?” Fraher said. Member Mary Elliott, 82, who also has Parkinson’s, was another one of the women to join the Tuesday class. Elliott joined the studio about a month ago. “I’m a weakling, and I decided I had to get stronger. And it’s been a terrific experience. They’re extremely nice, supportive, and helpful,” Elliott said of Fraher and Jones. ​ “I think it’s a great program for anybody interested in regaining their strength,” she added. ​Fraher and Jones also noted that many of their clients are grandparents working to stay strong to be able to take care of their grandchildren and spend time with them. “There are several people who are in that position, and it's a question of finding balance,” Jones said. “So, yes, those are great things for us to do for our families. But remember, you need to rejuvenate yourself in order to be able to do that.” ​ Anne Simeone, 70, another participant, said after the class that she started lifting weights about a year ago. She began working out with Fraher last year while she was still a trainer at the YMCA. A YMCA membership in Mystic costs $67 per month for adults and $59 per month for seniors, according to its website. Meanwhile, at “We Lift Heavy,” a monthly membership is $299 and a drop-in class is $30. But for members, the extra cost is worth it for the environment and personalized attention. “It was very busy. I couldn't always get on the machines when you wanted to get on them,” Simeone said of the YMCA. “So when Amy and Kathy opened up the studio, I followed them. I’m so happy I did because it's a great group of people. It's social, in addition to working out,” she added. Simeone explained that she started with just using the bar when she began lifting weights last year and has progressed to heavier weights over time. She was up to over 150 pounds on the leg press during Tuesday’s class. “I just started increasing little by little,” Simeone said. Aside from strength training, We Lift Heavy also has weekly yoga classes. Jones said she currently has a small group of people who regularly attend her classes. “And when I see how they come out of the class at the end, and they feel calm, and they can take on the day. As a teacher, it's fulfilling to see,” Jones said. Jones and Fraher also plan to hold other social events, including a holiday party, for people to hang out and enjoy the space. They’ve been together since 1992 and say they’ve seen the world change a lot in the 34 years they’ve been together. “We couldn’t get married back then … We’ve been through a lot together,” Fraher said. “In a world where there's not a whole lot of kindness and collectivity, we want to see that happen, at least for people who come here, so that they feel good about being together. Regardless of their perspective on the world,” Fraher added. We Lift Heavy is located at 12 River Road, Suite 1, in Pawcatuck, CT. Rio’s Junior Eurovision Song to be Revealed Next Week by Anthony Granger 20 September 2026 1 minute read Image source: RTP Salvador Rio’s song for the Junior Eurovision Song Contest 2026 in Ta’ Qali is set to be revealed in the coming week. RTP, the Portuguese public broadcaster, has announced that the nation’s entry for the Junior Eurovision Song Contest 2026 will be revealed next week. Salvador Rio recorded the song he will perform in Malta in July, with Diogo Piçarra confirmed as the songwriter. The title and details of the song that Salvador Rio will take to the Junior Eurovision stage in October have not yet been revealed. Inês Gonçalves represented Portugal at the Junior Eurovision Song Contest 2025 with “Para onde vai o amor?”. She finished 13th with 73 points. Source: RTP Portugal in the Junior Eurovision Song Contest + Portugal debuted at the 2006 edition of the Junior Eurovision Song Contest in Bucharest. The country placed second-last in 2006 and 2007 and withdrew in 2008. They did not return until 2017, when they were represented by Mariana Venâncio, who placed 14th with her song “YouTuber”. In 2024, Victoria Nicole finished 2nd for Portugal, its best ever result in the contest. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Darializa Avila Chevalie, center, is seen during a protest at the crime scene after an ICE officer allegedly shot a man in New York City on 8 October. Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPA View image in fullscreen Darializa Avila Chevalie, center, is seen during a protest at the crime scene after an ICE officer allegedly shot a man in New York City on 8 October. Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPA New York ‘Deeply concerning’: Democratic congressional candidate rebukes ICE’s presence in New York Darializa Avila Chevalier criticizes NYPD’s ‘inaction’ in protecting Marble Hill protesters after ICE shot a man Sanya Mansoor Sun 11 Oct 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 07.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Democratic congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier believes that the New York police departments’ conduct towards protesters after an ICE agent shot and wounded a man in the district she is running to represent violated “the spirit, if not the letter” of the city’s sanctuary laws . These rules ban local police from helping federal immigration authorities in civil immigration enforcement operations. Protests broke out in Manhattan’s Marble Hill neighborhood after a federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) agent shot Oscar Belgal, a 28-year-old Dominican man, while he was sitting in his car with a five-year-old in the backseat. The child was physically unharmed, and Belgal was taken to the hospital. He was reported as being in stable condition , before ICE reportedly took him into custody again. The Department of Homeland Security has said Belgal was undocumented. New York City’s Marble Hill residents furious after ICE shooting: ‘Why do this?’ Read more During Thursday night’s demonstration, which drew a few hundred New Yorkers , including Avila Chevalier, the NYPD set up barricades and clashed with protesters who were demanding ICE leave their neighborhood. Police had also helped carry Belgal to an unmarked car, where they laid him in the backseat while he was still handcuffed. Jessica Tisch, the New York City police commissioner, said during a Thursday press conference that the NYPD was not involved in the federal immigration operation prior to the shooting. Tisch said officers arrived for the purpose of preserving evidence. She also referred to Belgal’s previous criminal record during the event. Avila Chevalier said in a phone interview on Friday that the police commissioner’s mention of Belgal’s prior arrests unfairly villainized him and “showed that Tisch was more interested in peddling the narrative of the Trump administration than in upholding sanctuary policies”. The NYPD said in a statement that they always provide such information, and that many news outlets had asked about Belgal’s criminal history. Avila Chevalier also said the police’s “inaction” in protecting protesters was a failure to uphold the spirit of the city’s sanctuary laws. She wrote on X earlier on Friday: “The NYPD spent more time protecting a militia that just shot someone than protecting New Yorkers.” In the interview, Avila Chevalier appeared less concerned with the minutia of the city’s sanctuary law and more interested in getting rid of ICE entirely. “We wouldn’t need sanctuary policies if ICE didn’t exist,” she said. “The clearest solution here is the bold one: to demand that ICE be abolished.” We wouldn’t need sanctuary policies if ICE didn’t exist. The clearest solution here: demand ICE be abolished Mayor Zohran Mamdani also reiterated calls to abolish ICE and has referred to Thursday’s shooting as “unconscionable”. But he is facing pressure from progressives over reforming the NYPD in the wake of anti-ICE protests. Many immigration advocates, including Avila Chevalier, are calling for Tisch to step down and for the disbanding of the strategic response group (SRG), a rapid response unit within the NYPD that has been criticized for cracking down harshly on protests. Mamdani has repeatedly promised to disband the SRG, although that has not yet happened. He has so far shown no indication that he would remove Tisch from her role. Avila Chevalier acknowledged her differences with the mayor on these issues but noted: “It is my duty as someone who was elected to represent this district to echo the demands of people in my district,” she said. “I would not be a good partner to [Mamdani] if I weren’t doing that.” The mayor’s office did not respond to a request for comment. However, in an interview with the New York Times on Friday, Mamdani affirmed that Tisch would remain in charge of his police force but condemned officers’ aggression towards Avila Chevalier: “I do not think it is acceptable to throw anyone to the ground in our city,” he said. “I believe that to be true when it applies to the congresswoman-elect and, frankly, any New Yorker.” Avila Chevalier was on the front lines of Thursday’s protest, and videos circling social media showed her being knocked to the ground by a police officer . She says she “felt a hand grab and then throw [her] down to the ground”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines US Get the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion ‘Abolish ICE’: Mamdani, AOC and other Democrats urge action after New York shooting Read more “At some point, I felt like my feet were not touching the ground. I felt like I flew,” she said, adding that she is “thankfully OK” but was “in some pain” the day earlier. Avila Chevalier had said she was trying to convince police that adding barricades was escalating the situation: “They were literally in a tug of war with people over these barricades,” she said. “People were being hurt and pushed back.” The police arrested five protesters and said demonstrators “agitated and pushed over barriers” and “repeatedly refused verbal commands to disperse”. The NYPD also said that Avila Chevalier was pushed back by officers in an attempt to prevent the crowd from trampling the captain. On Friday, Avila Chevalier was distraught that Belgal’s lawyers had not been able to locate him. “That is deeply concerning to me,” she said. Avila Chevalier is a longtime organizer, who was also present at Columbia University’s pro-Palestine encampments , but said she isn’t used to this level of police aggression. She remains a strong believer in the impact of protest. “So much of the power given to our electeds comes from the space that constituents and organizers give us to be bold and to make those demands,” she said. “To know I was there with my community – that is what made me feel not only that I can do this but that this is what my community is demanding of us.” Explore more on these topics New York ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) US politics US immigration Democrats Trump administration US policing news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm89.text: Figure caption, Police: Three children and one teacher killed in Oregon school shooting By Rebecka Pieder Published 1 hour ago A 16-year-old fatally shot three children and a teacher at a primary school in the US state of Oregon before he was killed by a bystander. The unnamed attacker forced his way into Silver Rail Elementary School in the US city of Bend on Thursday afternoon by shooting at locked doors, police said. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said the teen was shot dead by "a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him". The three children killed were aged five, eight and 11. A seven-year-old and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to a hospital in a critical condition, police said. It is unclear if the assailant had any links to the school. Image source, Reuters Image caption, The suspected shooter was shot dead moments after local law enforcement arrived at the scene. "We are stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy," Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said in a statement. "No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing." Local law enforcement responded to reports of an active shooter at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, at 12:59 local time, Bend Police Department spokeswoman Sheila Miller told reporters. The first call indicated that an unknown suspect had shot into a car, she said. Photos released from the scene show a red truck with bullet holes. Minutes later, the local county dispatch received a flood of 911 calls and law enforcement were sent to the scene. The suspected shooter was shot dead at around 13:02pm, Miller said. While police said the shooter was a local 16-year-old boy, they declined to add further details pending the ongoing investigation.
